patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v3] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

version_history.subject: [PATCH v3] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch bypasses swap readahead for zswap, an in-memory synchronous backend similar to zram. The current implementation of swap readahead can lead to pointless prefetching of pages, causing increased anon residency and page cache thrashing. By bypassing readahead for zswap, the patch aims to reduce this overhead and improve performance. Measurements show significant gains in build time, zswap-in/out rates, and reduced swap readahead hits. The patch reuses existing code and adds a new helper function to check if a swap entry is synchronous.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Barry Song questioned whether the performance gain from bypassing swap readahead for zswap is dependent on the page-cluster setting, suggesting testing with values 0 and 1 to confirm

Reviewer Barry Song expressed interest in knowing if similar performance gains would be observed when using specific configurations, and suggested adding a mention of the 'page-cluster' configuration to the changelog.

Gave Reviewed-by
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

I assume your configuration is as below?

/ # cat /proc/sys/vm/page-cluster
3
/ # cat /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled
true

I am curious whether setting `/proc/sys/vm/page-cluster` to either 0
or 1 would result in the same performance gain on a zswap-enabled
system?

---

The change makes sense to me. I am just curious whether setting those
configurations would result in the same performance gain.

Maybe you can mention the `page-cluster` configuration in the changelog
as well.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: The reviewer notes a potential benefit of readahead for compressed swap, citing Kairui's LPC presentation, but acknowledges that this is not currently the case and assumes any future improvements would also apply to zswap.
review_comments.raw_body:
No objection here, I am just thinking about Kairui's LPC presentation
about how compressed swap can (in theory at least) still benefit from
readahead: https://lpc.events/event/20/contributions/2421/attachments/2116/4689/Better%20Anon%20(Swap)%20Readahead%20(2).pdf.

Seems like a big portion of the fault cost is still outside of
decompression and can benefit from readahead, but that isn't the case
today. I assume any future improvements to readahead and re-enabling
for zram would also cover zswap?

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/2] mm/zswap: batch the writeback IO

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/zswap: batch the writeback IO of consecutive entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the writeback I/O of zswap by batching consecutive entries into a single bio, reducing the number of I/O requests and improving performance. The patch introduces a new struct to share state between all entries written back in one LRU walk, allowing for more efficient use of I/O resources. The changes are based on measurements that show significant improvements in build time, write requests, pages per write request, iocost debt, and IO full pressure when batching is enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm/zswap: plug the writeback IO of an LRU walk
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the writeback IO of an LRU walk in the zswap module by allowing the block layer to merge pending writes that cannot be batched together. This is achieved by plugging the LRU walk, which reduces the number of write requests and improves performance. The patch includes benchmark results showing a 6.8% reduction in write requests and a 21.6% reduction in iocost debt when running alone, and a 4.6% reduction in write requests and a 10.6% reduction in IO full pressure when running next to a sibling fio random writer.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the writeback IO performance of zswap by batching consecutive entries and allowing the block layer to merge them. The patches modify the mm/zswap.c file, introducing a new LRU walk batch mechanism and plugging it into the existing code.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Expressed general approval of the patch series from a high-level perspective, but did not provide detailed technical feedback or analysis.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Oct 07, 2026 at 05:34:42PM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> Since commit 8f29aa226f82 ("mm/swap: introduce struct swap_io_ctx"),
> reclaim merges the swap writes of folios with consecutive slots into a
> single bio, but zswap writeback still issues one IO per entry. Patch 1
> makes each zswap LRU walk batch its writeback IO. Patch 2 plugs the
> walk, so that the block layer can merge what the batch cannot.

No a zswap expert, but from the high-level perspective this looks
great.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH v5 05/11] kernel/api: add API specification for sys_open
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch adds API specification for sys_open, which is a common practice to document function contracts and ensure they remain up-to-date. The discussion highlights the trade-off between placing documentation in headers or separate files, but ultimately decides to keep it in the header for better visibility.

review_comments.author: Serge Hallyn
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that long descriptions in API documentation will likely become outdated quickly due to their length, making them less useful even if kept separate from code.

Reviewer noted that relying on auto-generated documentation updates and flagging API breakages is more reliable than manually maintaining documentation, and suggested implementing an automation step to ensure consistency.
review_comments.raw_body:
OTOH these descriptions are so long that IMO they are guaranteed to go
stale anyway :)  While I'm editing a return value at the bottom of the
fn, most or all of the description is already going to be off my
terminal.

---

If every build auto-generates an update and then looks for and flags
meaningful changes (API breakages), then a) that is more reliable and b)
it doesn't matter where the docs are.

Even if there's just a three line comment above a fn, history proves
that it will not reliably stay in sync as the fn changes.  An automation
step/check is needed.

review_comments.author: Sasha Levin
review_comments.summary: Sasha Levin expressed concern that the API specification for sys_open should be separated from the code and placed elsewhere, such as in Documentation/, to prevent them from becoming stale and out of sync with the actual implementation.
review_comments.raw_body:
My plan is to be able to have the more detailed part of these specs somewhere
else, specially as they will grow some more, but I didn't want to add this
complexity right now.

review_comments.author: Serge Hallyn
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that documentation in code will inevitably become outdated and suggested moving it to a separate location where it can be automated
review_comments.raw_body:
My point was just that whether the docs are inline or not, they will go
stale without that automation.  So if that's the case, then the docs do
not need to be inline.

review_comments.author: Sasha Levin
review_comments.summary: reviewer suggested separating API specification from code by moving it to a different location, deferring the decision to the subsystem where those specs live
review_comments.raw_body:
Ah, sorry - got it.

The way I saw it working out is that the core part would be inline, but the
"speccy" part would move to a different location.  

Ultimately, this is the call of the subsystem where those specs live, and I see
different subsystems taking different approaches to this.

-- 
Thanks,
Sasha

review_comments.author: David Laight
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer David Laight expressed concern that the API specification for sys_open is placed in the .c file, which may lead to it becoming stale and out of sync with the code, and suggested keeping it in the header where it can be easily accessed by external users.

Reviewer David Laight expressed concerns that documenting API contracts in comments within code files is not effective, as it would require updating both the code and the comments simultaneously, leading to bloat and potential inconsistencies. He suggested instead documenting return values at the C return statement.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 8 Oct 2026 09:20:01 -0500
"Serge E. Hallyn" <serge@hallyn.com> wrote:

...

---

The only way it can possibly stay in step is to have the compiler process
the same source text.
Then, if you add/change a function parameter you'd be pretty much forced
to add/change the comment.
Return values would have to be documented at the C return statement and
really as an extra parameter to the return.

But, IMHO, the whole thing adds too much bloat to the source files.
When you 'grep' a source file, you don't really want another match in
a big comment at the top of every function.

David

review_comments.author: Serge Hallyn
review_comments.summary: Reviewer suggested moving API documentation to an autogenerated directory in Documentation/uapi/, which would ensure it stays up-to-date and provides warnings for changes.
review_comments.raw_body:
That's why I feel all this info that Sasha has added should go into a
Documentation/uapi/ autogenerated directory.  Auto-updated on every build,
with warnings if the result has changed.

-serge

review_comments.author: Sasha Levin
review_comments.summary: reviewer expressed neutrality on the placement of API documentation, noting that both approaches are acceptable and willing to reformat if requested by a maintainer
review_comments.raw_body:
I guess I don't mind either way: I heard both sides of this argument, and the
spec workflow is okay with either, so if the relevant maintainer asks for
changes here I'm more than happy to reformat this.

Which is, I think, the advantage here: it works just fine for the various
"kingdoms" we have in kernel-land.

-- 
Thanks,
Sasha
